title: v1: launch and status with TOML config, matching the current shell launcher
description:
## Why

Replace a personal shell launcher that grew Python snippets and broke twice. The launcher already makes the decision rota exists for; it needs to become a tested Rust tool with its personal details moved into a config file.

## Scope

- Backends:
  - agy (Antigravity CLI);
  - an sclaude-style second Claude account: `claude` run with its own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`;
  - Codex (`codex` with its own `CODEX_HOME`);
  - OpenCode;
  - the main Claude config as a last fallback.
- Quota readers per backend, borrowing the approaches in docs/references.md (caam, T3 Code's usage readers, OpenCode's Go usage schema, Codex's RateLimitSnapshot).
- One-at-a-time caps per backend through a process scan or a lock.
- Round-robin across available backends.
- Role and level to model (and effort) mapping in TOML.
- The guard check: refuse a backend whose configured command guard (for example dcg) is not installed.
- An atomic trusted-folder edit where a CLI needs it (agy stops at a trust prompt for an untrusted folder).
- `rota status --json`.
- `rota launch --dry-run`.

## Behavior reference

The reference is the personal shell launcher `agent-launch.sh` (kept outside this repository). Its behavior, without its personal paths or numbers:

- Usage: `[--role implement|review] [--level medium|high] [--only BACKEND] [--dry-run] <prompt file>`, run from the agent's working directory. Bad options or a missing prompt file exit 2.
- Level picks the model or effort: high maps to the top model or effort on each backend, medium to the next one down.
- Role picks the allowed backends: implementers may use agy, the second Claude account and Codex; reviewers only agy and the second Claude account. `--only` narrows the set and must be allowed for the role.
- Each backend check yields available or not, plus a reading line:
  - agy: requires the dcg guard hook in agy's hooks config, then reads `agy -p /usage` (tab-separated lines: group, limit name, "<n>%", reset time) and needs the five-hour and weekly remaining percentages of the "Claude and GPT models" group at or above per-role minimums.
  - Second Claude account: requires stored credentials; probes the usage endpoint with the stored access token; if the probe fails, wakes the account with one tiny prompt and probes again (never in a dry run, which must not spend a turn). Needs five-hour and seven-day used percentages under per-role limits; a missing window counts as under.
  - Codex: refuses in folders configured as belonging to another (work) account, runs an account check, then needs every quota window above 0% remaining.
- Caps: the second Claude account and agy each allow one running session at a time. A running session is found by scanning processes (the claude executable with that `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, including through a symlinked path; any agy process except a /usage probe).
- Round-robin: keeps the last pick in a state file and takes the first available backend after it, in a fixed order.
- No backend available: reviews and `--only` refuse (exit 3) with all readings; implementers fall back to the main Claude config, logged loudly.
- Every decision is logged with time, folder, role, level and all readings.
- `--dry-run` prints the pick and the command (the prompt shown as `$(cat file)`) and changes nothing, including the state file.
- Before launching agy, adds the folder to agy's `trustedWorkspaces` setting with an atomic write that keeps other keys and the file mode.
- Codex runs interactive and unattended, with approvals and sandbox off; the guard hook still checks every command.
- The launch replaces the launcher process (exec).

## Out of scope

- Mid-session failover.
- Account switching within one provider.
- Eon integration.

## Acceptance

- Unit tests for each quota parser, with fixtures of made-up data.
- Unit tests for the rotation and the caps.
- Unit tests for config validation.
- A dry run that matches the shell script's decision on the same readings.
- An example config in the repository with placeholder values only; personal paths, accounts and thresholds live in the user's config file.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test`
- One real launch of each backend in a scratch folder.

Keep backend names generic. OpenCode model and variant are command configuration. Reader and guard commands permit existing tools and proxy env without building a proxy. Missing Claude windows may be explicitly allowed.

description:
Lucca, 2026-11-06: "we are accumulating shell scripts again. cant we improve rota?" then "do it" to the overseer's proposal: rota absorbs the agent-lifecycle scripts the Eon overseer keeps writing (124 of them that day, 110 one-off copies). Each command must be generic (no Eon paths or policy in code; per-machine values in config.toml), allowlistable once, and shares the session registry planned in rota-1k7.

## What

`rota run`: a headless agent run (plan, review, investigate) for backends that have a non-interactive mode (Codex `codex exec` today; Claude `-p` later).

- stdin closed (a Codex review once hung two hours on stdin), a hard timeout, and the log and final report written under a rota run directory named by the session; the paths are printed and recorded in the session registry.
- Exit status reflects the run's; a timeout is reported as such.

Replaces: eon-overseer/codex-run.sh, codex-review.sh, codex-account-check.sh, start-planners.sh.

## Acceptance
- A run with a closed stdin, a timeout that fires, a guard refusal and a quota refusal, each tested.

- `$VAR` in arguments is passed literally (no expansion with `--scope`).
- A leader that called `pthread_exit` in its main thread shows `Z` with a live thread:
  `cgroup.events` says `populated 1` and `waitid(P_PID, WNOWAIT)` reports nothing until the
  unit is killed; then it reports SIGKILL.
- An unreaped zombie leader does not keep the scope populated.
- systemd quirk found by the tests: if the leader dies before systemd starts the scope, the
  scope stays `active` with an empty cgroup. rota stops an emptied scope (`systemctl --user
  stop --no-block`) when cleanup ends.

| --- | --- |

| 3 (first-record failure loses survivor info) | That path runs `stop`, reaps the leader only if it exited, and on survivors returns exit 125 with `ID cannot write session record: E; left processes running after SIGKILL: PIDS (unit U)`. |

### Overseer Decisions Recorded

1. Never treat an inspection failure as empty; unknown at the end of the kill phase is

### Verified Before Writing Code (2026-11-06)

- A zombie leader's `/proc/PID/cgroup` still names its scope, and once the scope's cgroup is
  removed it reads `0::PATH (deleted)`. So rota can tell, even after the leader exited,
  whether the leader ever joined the scope.
- If the unit name is taken, `systemd-run` exits 1 with `Unit … was already loaded` and never

| 3 systemd 258 expansion | `scoped` always passes `--expand-environment=no`. README: Linux 5.14+, cgroup v2, systemd 254+ (tested on 255). Regression `arguments_reach_the_command_literally` (`$HOME ${HOME} $$` arrives as-is). |

| 5 Unit-name collisions | `random()` is 128 bits from `getrandom(2)` as hex. `Scope::bind(leader)` binds only when the leader's `/proc/PID/cgroup` path ends in `/UNIT` (with or without ` (deleted)`): proof that this run's systemd-run created and joined the unit. A leader that exited without binding (systemd-run failed, e.g. the name was taken) gives outcome `failed`, exit 1, `could not start the run's scope; see LOG`. |

signals the leader before it joins the scope, so the case it covered (a scope started after
its leader died) only arises if systemd-run is still creating the scope at the end of the
grace and rota has to SIGKILL it. That may leave an empty, inert unit; it is not signalled, because rota

title: Read agy's 'disabled' quota row as exhausted and show when it resets
description:
## Why

When agy's "Claude and GPT models" weekly window is spent, `agy -p /usage` prints the
five-hour row as `disabled` instead of a percentage:

```
Claude and GPT models	Weekly Limit Remaining	0%	2030-01-08T14:00:00Z
Claude and GPT models	Five Hour Limit Remaining	disabled
```

`quota::parse` (`src/quota.rs`, `Parser::Agy`) rejects that row with
`invalid agy percentage`, so `rota status` shows `quota unreadable` for both roles. The
backend is still refused, but for the wrong reason: the owner cannot tell an exhausted
account from a broken reader, and rota never says when the backend comes back. The real
reason (weekly 0%) and its reset time are both in the output rota already reads.

## What

1. **Parse `disabled` as unavailable.** In the agy parser, a `disabled` value for a known
   window reads as 0% remaining. Any other non-percentage value stays an error.
2. **Keep the reset time.** The agy rows carry an RFC 3339 reset time in the fourth field.
   Keep it for each window, so a refusal can name it. A missing or malformed reset time is
   not an error: the window just has no reset time. Other parsers are unchanged unless
   carrying the reset is free for them.
3. **Show it.** When a role is refused because a window is under its limit, `rota status`
   (and the launch refusal message) names the window and, when known, its reset time, e.g.
   `weekly_left=0% (resets 2030-01-08T14:00:00Z)`. Keep the existing line shape otherwise.

## Out of scope

- Converting the reset to local time, or counting down.
- Reading the Gemini rows, or any change to how limits are configured.

## Verification

- Unit tests in `src/quota.rs` with made-up fixtures: the `disabled` five-hour row parses
  as 0% beside a 0% weekly row; a garbage value (`n/a`) is still an error; a row without a
  reset field parses with no reset.
- A test that the status/refusal text for an exhausted agy fixture names `weekly` and the
  reset time, and does not say `quota unreadable`.
- `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo test`.
